subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Continued Influence Effect: Retractions Don't Work
description: A quick win: understand The Continued Influence Effect: Retractions Don't Work.

hook.text: A news outlet reports that a warehouse fire was caused by arson. The next day, they retract: it was an electrical fault.

buildup.text: The continued influence effect: misinformation continues to shape thinking even after it's been corrected & the person.

discovery.text: Johnson & Seifert (1994) showed that retractions only partially reduce the influence of the original misinformation.

twist.text: The reason: retracting a fact leaves a gap in the mental model.

climax.text: Effective retractions provide an alternative explanation: 'It wasn't arson – it was a faulty wire.' The new story.

punchline.text: Don't just say 'that's wrong.' Say 'here's what actually happened.' Gaps get.

quiz.question: Why do retractions often fail to eliminate the influence of misinformation?
options: Retracting without providing an alternative leaves a gap that the old story fills
Retractions are always published too late

details.summary: The continued influence effect shows that misinformation continues to shape thinking even after people acknowledge a correction. Retracting false information does not undo its influence on memory and reasoning.
details.whyItMatters: This effect means that news corrections, scientific retractions, and legal instructions to disregard evidence systematically fail to remove the original misinformation's impact.
takeaways: Corrections do not erase the influence of initial misinformation
Providing an alternative narrative is more effective than simple retraction
Repetition of corrections can sometimes backfire by reinforcing the original claim

faq.question: Why do corrections often fail to change people's beliefs?
faq.answer: The original misinformation creates causal explanations in memory that persist independently. Removing the source leaves the explanation intact, and the brain prefers a wrong story to none.

faq.question: What is the most effective way to correct misinformation?
faq.answer: Provide a compelling alternative explanation that fills the causal gap, repeat the correct information more than the original falsehood, and avoid repeating the myth during correction.
